summary_text: Jasper Rabbit loved the carrots in Kraken Hopper field because they were big, crunchy, and free. He pulled carrots for snacks on his way to school, Little League practice, and home. After a game, Jasper heard a strange “tunk tunk tunk” sound and thought the carrots were following him. That night, he saw creepy carrots in his bathroom, but they disappeared when he looked again. The next day, he found no carrots at the field, but later he thought he saw them in the shed and on his bedroom wall. His parents searched and found nothing, so Dad said it was a bad dream. Soon Jasper saw creepy carrots everywhere. He decided they were real and made a plan to stop them. On Saturday, he took supplies to Kraken Hopper field. By sunset, his plan had worked: the carrots could not leave the patch. The carrots cheered because Jasper could not enter either, at least for now.

summary_text: A seed is in a bad mood because Halloween is his favorite holiday, but he has no costume. He tries being a ghost, vampire, and robot, but none works. He remembers fun costumes from past Halloweens, such as a rock band, condiments, and eggs, and worries that he cannot compete. The seed tricks everyone by announcing a storm and a herd of squirrels, so Halloween will be postponed. A pumpkin seed tells him Halloween is about leaves, decorations, togetherness, and community, not just costumes and candy. The seed realizes he has made too big a problem of his costume and has taken his bad mood out on others. He announces that Halloween is back on and admits his trick. He decides to worry less about things that do not matter. Later that evening, he dresses as a squirrel and joins the celebration. Everyone enjoys Halloween together.

summary_text: At Christmas, toys are nestled, tree lights glow, and stockings are stuffed. Santa gets his giant sack, but sees a note and snacks left by kind boys and girls. The dog finds Santa’s boots in the air and pushes, but Santa cannot move. The reindeer—Dasher, Dancer, Prancer, Vixen, Comet, Cupid, Donner, Blitzen, and Rudolph—make a chain and pull. On Santa’s command, everyone pushes and pulls. Santa pops free. The reindeer harness the sleigh, and Santa flies away, wishing everyone a Merry Christmas and good night.

summary_text: Long ago, Peg Leg Joe helped enslaved people escape. He worked on cotton plantations and taught them a secret song about following the drinking gourd, using the stars and trail signs to find freedom. When Molly’s husband, James, was sold away, they took their son Isaiah, Old Hattie, and young George and escaped that night. They walked by night and hid by day, avoiding slave catchers and hungry animals. They followed rivers, dead trees, and the stars. A farm boy shared bacon and cornbread with them. At the river’s end, Peg Leg Joe carried them across the wide Ohio River. Farmers then guided the five travelers along the Underground Railroad. They hid in a barn and later rested in a secret room at a Quaker farm. They traveled by foot and cart to Lake Erie. Finally, they boarded a steamship to Canada. Old Hattie said five more souls were safe when they reached freedom.

summary_text: Princess Ling loved her sister, Princess Myoshan. One morning, Myoshan left the palace through the window to escape an arranged marriage. Tomorrow, you will return as the kind King of Kindergarten.

summary_text: In Penguin City, Detective Waddles and his friend Flippers help penguins solve mysteries. One morning, Penny Puffin tells them that her beautiful eye sculptures are missing from her igloo. Waddles searches for clues, while Flippers uses an ice print detector. They find fish scales and a broken monocle. The clues lead them to the fish market, where Slick Mcbe says that fancy Sir Lushington bought ice cubes and wears a monocle. Sir Lushington explains that he dropped the monocle at Penny’s igloo and saw someone who smelled like fish and seaweed. Waddles knows this sounds like Captain Cod. At the docks, they follow Captain Cod into a warehouse and find the sculptures in crates. Captain Cod says he planned to trade them for fish. Waddles tells him stealing is wrong, so Captain Cod returns everything. Penny is happy, and Penguin City celebrates with a party. Waddles and Flippers return home, ready for new mysteries.

summary_text: On Monday, Mrs. Fibonacci tells the class that almost everything can be thought of as a math problem. On Tuesday, the narrator begins seeing math problems everywhere. Getting dressed, eating breakfast, catching the bus, counting shirts, and measuring things all make the narrator worry. At school, the number of students and desks leads to more problems. Lunch brings fractions because the pizza and apple pie are cut into equal pieces. Even art uses Mayan numerals, so the narrator feels like a math zombie. That night, the narrator dreams of being trapped in a room with only one piece of chalk. The narrator breaks it in half, puts the halves together, and uses the whole chalk to escape. On Wednesday morning, the narrator solves the time problem and breaks the Math Curse. Then Mr. Newton says that almost everything can be a science experiment and asks how the narrator has used math that day.

summary_text: Voting lets people choose and have a voice. People can vote by raising a hand, marking paper, or using a machine. The choice with the most votes wins. In the United States, people vote for the President and Vice President every four years. They also vote for senators, Congress people, mayors, sheriffs, and other leaders. The story explains that voting rights grew over time: Black men gained the right to vote in 1870, women in 1920, Native Americans in 1924, and 18-year-olds in 1971. Citizens who are at least 18 must register to vote. Political parties, such as Democrats and Republicans, choose candidates in primary elections. Candidates campaign with speeches, ads, debates, rallies, and visits. On Election Day, voters go to their assigned poll, often a school or firehouse, and vote in private. Votes are counted, and the Board of Elections announces the winner. The winner promises to serve everyone. The story ends by hoping readers vote for the Cat in the Hat.

summary_text: Mrs. Marta is a kind first-grade teacher at Sunnybrook Elementary. She bakes treats, helps her students learn, and makes them feel loved. But she also has loud, smelly, uncontrollable farts. They happen during math, reading, recess, and science, even when she tries to hold them in. Her students usually stay quiet, but during a school assembly, Mrs. Marta lets out her loudest fart. The children laugh, and Mrs. Marta feels very embarrassed. She runs away and stays home for three days. The class misses her, so Billy and Ashley help make a plan. The children create colorful cards, draw funny pictures, and practice a song about Mrs. Marta. Then they visit her house after school. They give her the cards and sing. Mrs. Marta hugs them and promises to return. The next day, she comes back to class. The children cheer and hug her, and they continue learning, sharing jokes, farts, and laughter together.

summary_text: G is a grape who remembers every hurt and holds a “Grudge.” A banana bumped G, an orange did not call back, and a lime kept G’s scarf. Long ago, G lived happily with about 3,000 grapes. G’s family taught kindness, forgiveness, consideration, gratitude, and staying sweet. Then G planned a big birthday party, but everyone came on the wrong day because G wrote May 31 instead of May 21. Nobody came, so G became bitter and sour. G held more and more grudges. Later, G was late meeting Lenny after bumping a knee, getting a flat tire, missing a bus, and leaving at the wrong stop. Lenny became angry and would not listen. Seeing Lenny act like G made G think differently. G noticed the peaceful park, found old family photos, and discovered the birthday mistake. G began talking, listening, and letting go of grudges. G apologized, forgave others, and became kinder, more grateful, and sweet again.

summary_text: The narrator and the other beans used to be one big pod of friends. Then some beans became the cool beans because they could play guitar, draw superheroes, or jump high. The narrator tried to look cool, but wore clothes that did not fit, walked into things, and was picked last. He felt ordinary and stopped trying. Later, the narrator missed a question in class, and everyone laughed. A cool bean whispered that the teacher wanted him to read page 32. These small acts made him feel better and gave him confidence. He began spending time with the cool beans again. He learned that being cool is not about looks. It is about helping, smiling, winking, nodding, and being there when someone needs a hand.

summary_text: Ronan was a mighty barbarian who led his people. He invaded, raided, and traded gold, jewelry, weapons, and tools. One day, he got a book, but no one wanted to trade for it. Ronan made library rules, gave out cards, recommended books, and read to the younglings. Ronan became a mighty librarian, and his people invaded, raided, and read.

summary_text: Nate the Great is a detective who works alone. After eating pancakes, he gets a call from Annie. She lost a yellow picture of her dog, Fang. Nate goes to her house and searches her yellow room, but the picture is not there. He watches Fang bury a bone, so he and Annie dig in the yard. They find no picture. Next, Nate talks to Rosamond, who has four cats. While leaving, he finds her lost cat, Super Hex, under his chair. Then Nate meets Annie’s brother, Harry, who paints him red. Nate looks at Harry’s paintings and notices that one monster is orange. He understands that Harry painted the red monster over Annie’s yellow picture of Fang. The yellow and red paint mixed together. The dog’s ears and tail became the monster’s three heads. Annie is upset, but she plans to paint a new picture. Nate eats pancakes, says goodbye, and walks home in the rain, glad he is wearing his rubbers.

summary_text: Alexander Hamilton was born in 1755 on Nevice. After his father left and his mother died, Alex became an orphan. He worked as a clerk and managed a company when he was only 14. After writing about a hurricane, rich businessmen sent him to college in America. In 1773, he arrived in Boston Harbor. England ruled the 13 colonies and taxed them, so Alex became a patriot. When the American Revolution began in 1775, he joined the army. He fought bravely and later became General Washington’s secretary. In 1781, Hamilton led an attack at Yorktown. The British lost, and the war ended. Hamilton then helped create the Constitution by writing essays to explain it. The states became one nation. President Washington made Hamilton Secretary of the Treasury. Hamilton helped create a national bank and money system. In 1804, Aaron Burr challenged him to a duel. Hamilton shot to miss, but Burr shot him, and Hamilton died the next day.

summary_text: A grape girl used to be sweet, kind, forgiving, and grateful. She lived with about 3,000 grapes in a close-knit Community, and her grandparents taught her to “stay sweet.” But on her birthday, she planned a huge party with rides, snacks, and fireworks, and nobody came. She became a sour grape girl who held grudges against everyone. One day, she was three hours late meeting her friend Lenny at the park because of several problems. Lenny became angry and refused to listen, just as she often did. Seeing his unfair anger helped her understand her own behavior. At home, she found an old photo of herself and then discovered that her party invitation said May 31st instead of May 21st. Nobody had come because she had written the wrong date. She began talking, listening, and letting go of grudges. She made peace with her friends and Lenny. Her sourness faded as she practiced kindness, forgiveness, consideration, and gratitude.

summary_text: Long ago, many people in New England celebrated Thanksgiving, but people in the South, West, and middle Atlantic states often ignored it. Thanksgiving was fading away, so it needed Sarah Hale. Sarah was a writer, mother, magazine editor, and strong supporter of schools, playgrounds, and other causes. Her secret weapon was her pen. She wrote letters and articles to persuade people to improve the world. Sarah loved Thanksgiving and wanted the whole country to celebrate it on the same day. She wrote thousands of letters, and states began making Thanksgiving a holiday. She then wrote to presidents Zachary Taylor, Millard Fillmore, Franklin Pierce, and James Buchanan, but each refused. During the Civil War, Sarah wrote to Abraham Lincoln. She explained that Thanksgiving could help bring the country together. Lincoln agreed. In 1863, he made Thanksgiving a national holiday. After 38 years of work, Sarah Hale saved Thanksgiving.

summary_text: A seed visits the library, his favorite place. He enjoys the books, kind librarians, comfy chairs, and big windows. The seed feels like a hero and chooses another book to read. He discovers that finding a new book is part of the adventure of reading. Soon, he finds a new favorite book. Two weeks later, another letter arrives, and he cries, “Oh no,” because the new book is due too.

summary_text: Pret Hemman lived in a village built on stilts. Before school, he helped his father load the Longboat for fishing, but Pret dreamed about soccer. He and his friends played on a sandbar when the tide was low, until rising waves covered it. While watching the World Cup at Uncle’s coffee shop, the boys decided to build their own field. They collected wood, barrels, and styrofoam and worked for weeks. Their floating field had fish neck goals, but loose boards and water made playing difficult. Villagers first called them crazy, then stopped to watch and cheer. When a mainland tournament was announced, families gave the boys matching jerseys, shorts, and cleats, forming the py football club. The team won several games and reached the semifinals. Heavy rain flooded the grass field, so the boys removed their shoes and played barefoot, as they did at home. They lost by one goal but finished third. Back home, they could play whenever they wanted.

After school, he and his friends played on a sandbar until the rising tide covered it. While watching the World Cup at Uncle’s coffee shop, the boys decided to make their own field. They collected wood, barrels, and styrofoam, then built a floating field with fish neck goals. At first, villagers thought they were crazy, but later they stopped to watch and cheer. When the boys heard about a mainland tournament, their families gave them matching jerseys, shorts, and cleats. The Py football club won several games and reached the semifinals. Heavy rain flooded the grass field, so the boys removed their shoes and played barefoot, as they did on their floating field. They scored twice but lost by one goal. They came in third place and returned home happily, ready to keep playing on their floating field.

He asks 8, but she knows nothing and disguises herself as zero. At Cafe Uno, waitress B says that 9 has disappeared. The detective then visits 11, who says 7 could not have done it. On his way back, the detective sees someone crossing the street and understands the mystery. At his office, he finds 6 taking forty winks. He turns 6 upside down and discovers that his client is really 9. The detective learns that 9 blamed 7 because 7 gets attention from things like the Seven Wonders of the World and the seven seas. Seven and 9 make peace, and the numbers return to order. The next day, 2 calls the detective with another problem: she needs to change her number.
